Hi Asha — appreciate the context and the usage file. Below are three viable structures we typically propose; I’ve called out trade-offs so your procurement team can pick what matters most (predictability vs. flexibility).

Option 1 — 12-month, staged-commit (no auto-renew):
- Term: 12 months (co-term to 12/31/2027)
- Pricing: list price; 5% credit in month 1–3 if usage < 50% of committed capacity
- Ramp: Month 1 = 30% committed, Month 4 = 60%, Month 7 = 85%, Month 10+ = 100%
- Good if you want to keep renewal cadence yearly and avoid auto-renew.

Option 2 — 24-month, co-term with ramp credits (recommended middle ground):
- Term: 24 months, co-term to 12/31/2028 (prorated first partial year)
- Pricing: 12% discount vs list; ramp credit schedule to offset unused committed capacity in first 6 months
- Ramp schedule (example): Month 1–3: 25% billed capacity, Month 4–6: 50%, Month 7–12: 75%, Month 13+: 100%
- Auto-renew: OFF by default; we provide price protection for the 24 months without auto-renew clause.
- Good for smoothing unit economics while keeping contractual control.

Option 3 — 36-month, multi-year commit (requires auto-renew or early-termination carve):
- Term: 36 months, deeper 18% discount; requires either auto-renew or a modest early-termination fee to protect pricing
- Ramp: Largest credits in first 9 months; aggressive unit-cost savings thereafter
- Best if you plan predictable high growth and want max price certainty.

Next steps I suggest: pick the option you prefer; we can produce a one-page amendment showing the co-term/pricing and a month-by-month ramp (I attached a sample ramp schedule + editable spreadsheet). If you pick Option 2, I’ll loop in Pricing/Finance and produce the amendment for signature.

Proposed immediate ask: are you leaning Option 1/2/3?
